chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about a man who deliberately broke his fast for one day in the month of Ramadan, so he said:

"Indeed, a man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'I am ruined, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'What is wrong with you?' He said, 'Hellfire, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'What is wrong with you?' He said, 'I had intercourse with my wife.' He said, 'Give charity and seek forgiveness from your Lord.' The man said, 'By He who has magnified your right, I did not leave in the house anything small or large.' A man from the people entered with a measure of dates containing twenty sa's, which is ten asw'uq by our sa'. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Take these dates and give charity with them.' He said, 'O Messenger of Allah, with whom shall I give charity, when I have told you that I have neither little nor much in my house?' He said, 'Then take them and feed your family, and seek forgiveness from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.' He said, 'And when we returned, our companions said, 'Indeed, he began with manumission.' He said, 'Manumit, or fast, or give charity.'"

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for deliberately breaking the fast in Ramadan due to intercourse?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the *kaffarah* for deliberate intercourse during Ramadan, establishing a hierarchical sequence of expiation: freeing a slave, fasting sixty consecutive days, or feeding sixty poor people. The narrative highlights the Prophet’s (peace be upon him and his family) practical jurisprudence, showing how the obligation adapts to the individual's financial capacity, as seen when the companion was instructed to feed his own family after failing to find a specific recipient for charity. This incident underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the flexibility of *kaffarah* methods based on economic ability, a principle derived from the Quranic verse 'And for those who can fast only with great difficulty, a ransom [is due]...' (2:184).
